title: How to Choose the Right Data Analytics Course in Tirupati for Beginners
summary:
Choosing a data analytics course can be confusing, especially when you are a beginner with little or no technical experience. You may find several training options, but how do you know which one will actually help you develop practical skills? Before enrolling, it is important to understand which tools you need to learn, how practical training works and what makes a course suitable for your career goals. This guide explains what beginners should consider when selecting data analytics training in Tirupati.

Understand What Data Analytics Involves
Data analytics is the process of collecting, organising and examining information to identify patterns and support better decisions. Businesses use data analytics to understand customer behaviour, monitor sales, improve operations and identify opportunities.
For example, a retail business can analyse its monthly sales records to identify popular products, compare revenue and understand customer purchasing patterns. This shows how analytical skills can be applied to everyday business situations.
Which Skills Should a Beginner Learn?
Before choosing a Data Analytics Course, understand whether the curriculum covers the essential tools and concepts.
1. Microsoft Excel
Excel helps beginners organise information, use formulas, create pivot tables and prepare reports. It is a useful starting point for understanding structured data.
2. SQL
SQL helps analysts access and work with data stored in databases. Beginners should learn how to write queries, retrieve specific records, filter data and combine information from multiple tables to find meaningful insights.
3. Python
Python supports data cleaning, processing and analysis. Libraries such as Pandas and NumPy help learners work with datasets more efficiently.
4. Power BI
Power BI helps transform data into interactive dashboards and visual reports. It allows users to communicate findings in a clear and understandable way.
5. Basic Statistics
Understanding averages, percentages, distributions and trends helps learners interpret data correctly rather than simply presenting numbers.
Why Should You Look for Practical Training?
Learning tool definitions is not enough to understand how analytics works. Beginners need opportunities to practise with datasets and solve realistic problems.
For example, a student can work on a sample sales analysis project by organising records in Excel, querying information through SQL, analysing data using Python and presenting results through a Power BI dashboard.
These activities help learners understand how different tools work together. They also provide useful project experience that can be included in a professional portfolio.
How to Select the Right Training Institute in Tirupati
Before enrolling in a Data Analytics Course in Tirupati, compare training options using these factors:
• Check whether the syllabus covers relevant analytics tools.
• Ask whether practical assignments and real-world projects are included.
• Understand the trainer's teaching approach and technical experience.
• Check whether doubts and technical challenges receive proper guidance.
• Look for resume preparation and interview guidance.
• Understand the course duration, fees and learning support before making a decision.
Do not choose a course only because it offers a certificate. Focus on the quality of learning and practical exposure.

Students and graduates looking for structured learning can explore the Data Analytics training program at Takeoff Learnings. The course covers important areas such as Excel, SQL, Python, Statistics and Power BI, helping learners develop a foundation in analytical tools and practical concepts.

title: Building Sovereign Multi-Agent Orchestration & DAG State Machines in Pure Python: Kahn's Algorithm, Dynamic Routing & Checkpointing
summary:
In modern artificial intelligence engineering, single-prompt LLM execution has hit an architectural plateau. Real-world enterprise challenges—such as autonomous codebase generation, financial quantitative research, and complex customer fulfillment—require specialized autonomous agents collaborating in choreographed workflows.

Yet mainstream orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI) have introduced staggering operational liabilities:

  • Fragile Dependency Bloat: Installing them pulls dozens of conflicting packages, frequently triggering breaking version changes.
  • Opaque Abstractions: Debugging recursive state loops, hidden serialization overhead, and thread locks becomes a nightmare.
  • Artificial Latency: Internal framework serialization introduces tens of milliseconds of unnecessary lag per tool call.

In this deep architectural breakdown, we engineer AgentGraph Pro: an enterprise-grade, sovereign multi-agent workflow orchestrator in 100% pure Python delivering 76,065 workflows/second, sub-13µs execution latency, Kahn's topological cycle detection, and zero external dependencies.

1. The Geometry of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)

Workflows in multi-agent systems are modeled as directed graphs where nodes represent agent tasks and directed edges represent state transitions:

[Entry Point: Planner Agent]
             │
             ▼
    [Researcher Agent]
             │
             ▼
      [Critic Agent]
        /        \
       /          \
[Approved == True]  [Approved == False]
     │                      │
     ▼                      ▼
[Publisher Agent]    [Reviser Agent]

To guarantee execution safety and eliminate infinite recursion before runtime, the graph compiler executes Kahn's Algorithm for topological sorting:

$$\text{Time Complexity} = O(V + E)$$

from collections import defaultdict, deque
from typing import Dict, List, Set

class DAGEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def validate_and_sort(nodes: Set[str], edges: List[Edge]) -> List[str]:
        in_degree: Dict[str, int] = {n: 0 for n in nodes}
        adj: Dict[str, List[str]] = defaultdict(list)

        for edge in edges:
            if edge.condition is None:
                adj[edge.source].append(edge.target)
                in_degree[edge.target] += 1

        queue = deque([n for n, deg in in_degree.items() if deg == 0])
        ordered: List[str] = []

        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            ordered.append(u)
            for v in adj[u]:
                in_degree[v] -= 1
                if in_degree[v] == 0:
                    queue.append(v)

        if len(ordered) != len(nodes):
            remaining = [n for n in nodes if in_degree[n] > 0]
            raise ValueError(f"Cycle detected in static graph among nodes: {remaining}")

        return ordered

2. Dynamic State Graphs & Conditional Edge Routing

Unlike rigid linear chains, intelligent agent graphs evaluate dynamic state predicates at runtime:

builder = StateGraph()
builder.add_node("planner", plan_action)
builder.add_node("researcher", search_action)
builder.add_node("critic", quality_gate)
builder.add_node("publisher", deploy_action)

builder.set_entry_point("planner")
builder.add_edge("planner", "researcher")
builder.add_edge("researcher", "critic")

# Dynamic Quality Gate:
builder.add_conditional_edge(
    "critic",
    condition=lambda state: state.get("approved", False),
    target_true="publisher",
    target_false="reviser"
)

3. Snapshot Checkpointing & Human-In-The-Loop (HITL)

In mission-critical enterprise deployments, workflows must survive server restarts and support Human-In-The-Loop authorization:

  1. Atomic Checkpointing: Every node execution step captures a JSON-serializable snapshot of the entire typed state dictionary.
  2. Approval Barriers: Sensitive operations (e.g., executing financial trades or deleting database records) pause execution, commit the checkpoint to disk, and await human webhook confirmation without holding thread connections open.
  3. Time-Travel Resumption: Workflows can be replayed, audited, or branched into hypothetical counterfactual paths from any historical step $N$.

title: I built a one-click installer for local LLMs on Windows: it picks a model for your hardware and sets up Ollama
summary:
Running an LLM locally is not hard, but the first time is a small quest: install Ollama, figure out which of a hundred models fits your GPU, get the tag right, wait for gigabytes to download, find a UI. I kept getting asked to set this up for friends, so I built Local AI: a free, open-source (MIT) Windows app that looks at your hardware, picks a model, installs Ollama and the model, and opens a chat.

What it does

  • One LocalAI.exe (about 42 MB), no Python or anything else to install first.
  • Detects the GPU, VRAM, RAM and free disk space, and recommends a model from a catalogue of 34 (Qwen3, Gemma 3/3n, Llama 3.1/3.2, Mistral, Phi-4, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen2.5-Coder and -VL, LLaVA, gpt-oss).
  • Downloads and installs Ollama without administrator rights, then pulls the model with progress.
  • Chat with streaming replies, a "think" mode, attachments (text files, and images for vision models), and an "about this model" panel.
  • Choose folders for Ollama and models, move models to another drive, update everything, and remove it all without a trace.
  • English and Russian UI, two themes.

Conversations never leave the PC: the chat talks to Ollama on 127.0.0.1. The network is only used for downloads and update checks.

How it is built

It is Python plus pywebview (WebView2). main.py starts a local HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 and opens the window; the UI is plain HTML/CSS/JS with no build step. API requests are protected by a per-session token header and a Host check, so a web page in your browser cannot call the local server.

Some parts were more fun than I expected:

  • Hardware detection without WMI. WMI is broken on my machine and probably on some of yours, so the GPU comes from nvidia-smi or the display-class registry key, and RAM from GlobalMemoryStatusEx via ctypes.
  • Model choice. Each catalogue entry has a size and a rough memory estimate (file size x 1.2 + 0.6 GB). If it fits in VRAM it is a GPU model, if it fits in 70% of RAM it runs mixed or on CPU, otherwise it is hidden.
  • Resumable download of the 1.6 GB Ollama installer with Range requests, plus a signature check before running it.
  • No stray console windows: ollama serve must be started with CREATE_NO_WINDOW and without DETACHED_PROCESS, otherwise every child process opens its own black console.

Limits and download

Windows 10/11 only. Without a GPU it runs on the CPU, slower and with a smaller model. The app is not code-signed, so SmartScreen may ask you to confirm ("More info" → "Run anyway"), and some antivirus tools dislike PyInstaller executables; the source is open if you prefer to build it yourself.

  • Download (about 43 MB): https://github.com/OlegChe77/local-ai/releases/latest/download/LocalAI.zip
  • Source (MIT): https://github.com/OlegChe77/local-ai

I'd love to hear what is missing or broken. Issues and comments are welcome.

title: Your Reset Tokens Came From Python's random and Someone Collected Enough to See the Next One
summary:
The password reset
worked like everyone's.

Click forgot,
get an email,
follow a link
with a token on the end.

Eight hex characters.

Someone had written it years ago
in one line.

random.getrandbits of thirty two,
formatted as hex.

It looked random.

Every token was different.

Nobody could guess one
by looking at the others.

Nobody human.

Python's random module
is a Mersenne Twister.

It is a very good generator
for simulations,
for shuffling,
for tests.

It was never meant
to keep a secret.

Its entire future
is decided by its internal state,
six hundred and twenty four numbers
of thirty two bits.

And every output it gives you
is one of those numbers,
lightly scrambled
in a way that can be undone.

So if you see
six hundred and twenty four outputs in a row,
you can rebuild the state.

Then you are the generator.

I tried it.

A server seeded from the operating system,
six hundred and twenty four tokens read off it,
each one unscrambled,
loaded into a fresh copy.

The next three tokens
from both of them
matched,
character for character.

Now picture the attacker.

He makes an account.

He asks for a reset
six hundred and twenty four times,
which your system allowed,
because it was his own account.

Then he asks for a reset
on someone else's.

The email goes to them.

The token
he already knows.

The Python documentation
says it plainly,
near the top of the page.

Do not use this module
for security purposes.

Use secrets.

secrets.token_urlsafe
reads from the operating system's
cryptographic source,
and seeing a million of its outputs
tells you nothing
about the next one.

So search your code
for random,
and read every place it is used
for a token,
a password,
an invite code,
a session.

Make tokens long,
single use,
and short lived.

Store only their hash.

And rate limit the reset form,
because even a good token
should not be
something you can ask for
six hundred times an hour.

Random enough to look at
is not
random enough to bet on.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: You Scheduled One Job per Region and Every Job Ran for the Last One
summary:
The nightly report
used to be one big job.

You split it up,
one job per region,
so a slow region
would not hold up the rest.

Three regions.

North, south, west.

A loop,
and inside it
a small lambda
handed to the scheduler.

for region in regions,
add a job
that builds the report for region.

It looked right.

It read right.

At six in the morning
three reports arrived.

All three said west.

North and south
got the west numbers,
with their own names
in the subject line.

Nothing crashed.

The scheduler did exactly
what it was given.

The lambda did not keep
the region it was born with.

It kept the name.

Region.

A name that lives
in the scope around it,
and is looked up
when the function runs,
not when it was made.

By the time the scheduler ran anything,
the loop had long finished,
and region meant west,
for everyone.

It is called late binding,
and Python is not alone.

JavaScript did the same
with var in a loop,
until let gave each turn
its own variable.

Python has no let.

A list comprehension
does not save you either.

I ran it both ways.

Three lambdas,
three times the word west.

Your tests did not see it
because they called the function
straight away,
inside the loop,
while region still meant
the region they expected.

The bug only exists
when there is a gap
between making the function
and calling it.

And a gap
is the whole point
of a scheduler,
a callback,
a button handler,
a retry.

So bind the value
at the moment you mean it.

Use functools.partial,
which stores the argument itself,
not the name.

Or write a small function
that takes the region
and returns the job,
so each call
gets a fresh scope to keep.

And when a loop
hands functions to something
that will call them later,
test it later.

Collect the jobs first.

Run them after the loop.

Check each one
did its own work.

A closure does not remember
what a variable was.

It remembers where to look.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

It read right.

at the moment you mean it.

not the name.

so each call

hands functions to something
that will call them later,
test it later.

Collect the jobs first.

Run them after the loop.

Check each one
did its own work.

A closure does not remember
what a variable was.

It remembers where to look.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: How to Audit a Vendor’s Backtest Before You Pay a Single Rupee
summary:
You are not the one who built the strategy — you are the one being asked to pay for it. That makes you the auditor. Here is the buyer-side checklist, in order.

Almost everything written about backtest validation is written for the person building the strategy. But if you are considering paying for one — a bot, a signal service, a course strategy, a “proven” model — you are not the builder. You are the buyer. And the buyer needs a different checklist, because the builder’s incentives run the other way.

Here it is, in order. Any vendor who fails the first three is done.

1. Show me the raw predictions

Not a screenshot. Not an equity curve. The raw file: predictions with timestamps, and the actual outcomes. If you cannot recompute the accuracy yourself — or have it recomputed — from raw predictions, you have nothing verifiable. A claimed-accuracy column in a vendor’s file is the easiest number in finance to inflate, which is why any serious check ignores it and recomputes from the predictions themselves.

2. How many did you try — and where are the losers?

The trial count is the single most predictive question in this whole field. A vendor who tried 500 versions and shows you the best is showing you a lottery winner. Ask for the number, and ask to see the discarded versions. A vendor who cannot or will not answer has answered.

3. What do the dumb baselines score?

Always-bullish and no-change, on the same data. If the vendor’s model cannot beat both, it adds nothing — it is riding the base rate. On a bare CSV with no price history, those two baselines are the honest ones; anything claiming five baselines without price history is faking three of them.

4. Show me the folds, not the average

A single overall accuracy hides decay. Ask for walk-forward results fold by fold, earliest to latest. A model decaying from 80% to 56% across folds is a dying edge with a flattering average. Also ask which version of “walk-forward” they mean: period stability (accuracy across time periods) or purged, embargoed training (leak-proof fold construction). Vendors who say “walk-forward validated” without saying which have told you nothing precise.

5. What did it cost — in the backtest?

Commissions, spread, slippage, taxes. A backtest with zero costs is a fantasy. Ask for net-of-cost results, and ask at what slippage the edge dies (the break-even cost per trade). If the edge survives only at zero friction, it does not survive.

6. What market regime was this?

A strategy that only worked in one regime — one trend, one volatility environment — is a bet on that regime repeating. Ask for results sliced by year and by regime. Concentration in one slice is a warning, not a track record.

7. Can I forward-test before paying?

The strongest answer a vendor can give is: “Here is a forward-test window — paper-trade it live for 30 days and watch.” The weakest is pressure to pay now for a backtest you cannot reproduce. Time is the cheapest audit there is.

The sentence that ends most pitches

“I’d like the raw prediction file, the trial count, the baseline scores, and the fold-by-fold results. If those check out, I’ll forward-test before paying.”

Most vendors will not survive that sentence. The ones who do are the only ones worth a second conversation — and they are rare, which is exactly why the sentence works.

BuildIT Index exists so you can run that sentence mechanically: hand it a prediction file, get a recomputed accuracy, baseline scores, walk-forward folds, leakage gate, multiple-testing correction, calibration, and a verdict with an exit code. The tool does the audit; you make the decision.

The buyer who asks the right questions rarely needs to pay for the wrong answer.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past backtest results do not predict future returns.

title: Find broken links on your website for free (and fail CI when new ones appear)
summary:
Broken links pile up quietly. A partner renames a page, a docs section moves, or a typo slips into a Markdown file. Visitors hit 404s and search engines waste crawl budget long before anyone notices.

This post covers:

  1. A minimal link checker in plain Python (no dependencies) that crawls your site and checks every link.
  2. Why naive checkers report false positives, and how to avoid them.
  3. A hosted crawler that does this at scale, with a weekly GitHub Actions check that fails when something breaks.

Disclosure: I built the Broken Link Checker Actor used in part 3. Parts 1 and 2 don't need it.

1. A minimal checker (Python standard library) 

import sys
import urllib.request
from collections import defaultdict, deque
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.parse import urljoin, urldefrag, urlparse

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (link-check script)"}

class Links(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.links = []
    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag == "a":
            href = dict(attrs).get("href")
            if href:
                self.links.append(href)

def get(url, method="GET"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA, method=method)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
            ctype = r.headers.get("Content-Type", "")
            body = r.read() if method == "GET" and "html" in ctype else b""
            return r.status, body
    except HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, b""
    except (URLError, TimeoutError) as e:
        return f"error: {getattr(e, 'reason', e)}", b""

def crawl(start, max_pages=20):
    host = urlparse(start).netloc
    found_on = defaultdict(set)          # link -> pages that contain it
    queue, seen, pages = deque([start]), {start}, 0
    while queue and pages < max_pages:
        page = queue.popleft()
        code, body = get(page)
        pages += 1
        p = Links()
        p.feed(body.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
        for href in p.links:
            link = urldefrag(urljoin(page, href))[0]
            if not link.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
                continue                 # mailto:, tel:, javascript:
            found_on[link].add(page)
            if urlparse(link).netloc == host and link not in seen:
                seen.add(link)
                queue.append(link)
    return found_on

def check(link):
    code, _ = get(link, "HEAD")
    if isinstance(code, str) or code >= 400:   # many servers mishandle HEAD: confirm with GET
        code, _ = get(link)
    return link, code

if __name__ == "__main__":
    site = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "https://www.scrapethissite.com"
    found_on = crawl(site)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(check, found_on))
    broken = [(l, c) for l, c in results if isinstance(c, str) or c >= 400]
    print(f"checked {len(results)} links, {len(broken)} broken")
    for link, code in broken:
        print(code, link, "<- found on", sorted(found_on[link])[0])
    sys.exit(1 if broken else 0)

How it works:

  • It crawls same-host pages breadth-first, up to max_pages, and collects every .
  • It remembers where each link was found. A list of broken URLs is much less useful if you still have to search the site for them.
  • It checks each unique link with HEAD and confirms failures with GET (more on why below).
  • It exits with code 1 if anything is broken, so it works as a CI step.

Run it:

python linkcheck_stdlib.py https://your-site.example

2. Why naive link checkers lie

The first version of my script sent only HEAD requests and flagged links that load fine in a browser. These are the usual causes:

  • HEAD is often handled badly. Some servers return 405, 404 or even 500 for HEAD but serve the page fine with GET. Always confirm a failure with GET before reporting it.
  • Bot protection is not breakage. LinkedIn returns 999, many sites behind Cloudflare return 403 or a challenge page, and others return 429 when you're too fast. Report these separately as "blocked", not "broken", or you'll get used to ignoring the report.
  • Redirects matter. A 301 that ends in a 200 isn't broken, but internal links that redirect, and especially redirect chains (http → https → www → /new-path), are worth fixing. Record the chain, not just the final status.
  • Politeness. Firing 50 parallel requests at a small shared host gets you rate-limited and causes false alarms. Limit concurrency per host, set timeouts, and respect robots.txt for the pages you crawl.
  • Scope. Images, scripts and stylesheets break too, but checking them multiplies the request count. Make it opt-in.

The script in part 1 covers the first point. The others are where most of the work in a real checker goes.

3. Hosted option: Broken Link Checker on Apify

The Broken Link Checker crawls your site (or checks a list of URLs) and records every link as ok, redirect, broken, timeout or blocked. title: MinTRL: How Long a Track Record Do You Actually Need?
summary:
A Sharpe ratio of 2.0 on 18 months of data proves almost nothing. Minimum Track Record Length turns “impressive Sharpe” into “how many years would this take to believe” — with the numbers.

A strategy shows a Sharpe ratio of 2.0. Your instinct says “excellent.” The correct response is a question: over how long?

Minimum Track Record Length (MinTRL) is the answer to that question, formalised. It asks: given an observed Sharpe ratio, how many years of track record would you need before you could believe, with 95% confidence, that the true Sharpe is above zero — that the strategy is better than nothing at all?

The idea comes from the same research tradition as the deflated Sharpe ratio (Bailey and López de Prado), and it is brutally clarifying, because it converts a sexy number into a boring one: years.

Why short track records prove so little

Returns are noisy. A high Sharpe over a short window can easily be luck — a few good months, a favourable regime, a lucky draw. The shorter the window, the wider the uncertainty around the Sharpe, and the longer the track record you would need to shrink that uncertainty to something believable.

The relationship runs the way you would hope it does not: the more modest the Sharpe, the longer the record needed. As an anchored example from the reference literature, a Sharpe of around 0.95 on daily data needs roughly 3 years of history to clear the 95% confidence bar. Lower Sharpes need longer; higher Sharpes need less — but even a Sharpe of 2.0 on a year and a half of data is thinner evidence than it looks, and once you correct for the number of strategies tried (the multiple-testing problem), the required length grows further. In some published multi-market reviews, the required length for the observed Sharpes was effectively infinite — the data could not support the claim at any reasonable horizon.

The trial-count trap inside MinTRL

Here is the part vendors never mention: MinTRL assumes the Sharpe you see is the Sharpe of one strategy, honestly measured. If the vendor tried 200 strategies and shows you the best, the relevant Sharpe is deflated first — and the deflated Sharpe needs a longer track record than the advertised one. A Sharpe of 2.0 that deflates to 0.6 under a multiple-testing correction does not need months of belief. It needs years.

So the two questions always travel together: “What is the Sharpe?” and “How many did you try?” A MinTRL quoted without a trial count is a half-answer.

How to use MinTRL tomorrow

When a vendor quotes a Sharpe, ask for the track record length in years and the number of trials. Then ask what MinTRL their own numbers imply. If they cannot answer, they have not done this math — and you should do it for them, conservatively.

Treat any Sharpe above 3.0 on a short record as a red flag, not a selling point. Extreme Sharpes on short samples are the signature of overfitting, not genius.

Remember that MinTRL is about statistical belief, not profitability. A strategy can clear MinTRL and still lose money to costs, slippage, and regime change. It is one gate among several: recompute, baselines, walk-forward folds, leakage, trial correction, and then track-record length.

The honest summary: most strategies you are shown have not existed long enough, on their own numbers, to be believed. MinTRL just makes that sentence quantitative — and once you see it in years, you cannot unsee it.

A Sharpe of 2.0 on 18 months is a claim. A Sharpe of 2.0 on 5 years with a known trial count is evidence. MinTRL turns the first into the second.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past backtest results do not predict future returns.

title: Extract every URL from a sitemap (incl. sitemap indexes and .xml.gz) and check status codes
summary:
You need a list of every URL on a site, whether that's for an SEO audit, a migration redirect map, a crawl seed list or chunks for a RAG pipeline. The sitemap is the obvious place to start. In practice "the sitemap" is often:

  • listed in robots.txt, or not at all,
  • a sitemap index pointing at 5–500 child sitemaps,
  • gzipped (sitemap-1.xml.gz), sometimes without a Content-Encoding header, and
  • full of URLs that redirect or return 404.

This post builds a small, dependency-free Python script that handles all four. It then shows a hosted version for when you need filters, many sites or a schedule.

Disclosure: I built the Sitemap URL Extractor Actor shown in part 2. Part 1 is plain Python, so use it freely.

1. Do it yourself: Python standard library only 

import gzip
import urllib.request
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.parse import urljoin

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (sitemap-check script)"}
NS = "{http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9}"

def fetch(url):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA), timeout=30) as r:
        body = r.read()
    if body[:2] == b"\x1f\x8b":  # gzip magic bytes (.xml.gz), regardless of headers
        body = gzip.decompress(body)
    return body

def find_sitemaps(site):
    """Sitemap: lines in robots.txt, falling back to /sitemap.xml."""
    try:
        robots = fetch(urljoin(site, "/robots.txt")).decode("utf-8", "replace")
        found = [l.split(":", 1)[1].strip() for l in robots.splitlines()
                 if l.lower().startswith("sitemap:")]
        if found:
            return found
    except (HTTPError, URLError):
        pass
    return [urljoin(site, "/sitemap.xml")]

def walk(sitemap_url, seen=None, max_sitemaps=50):
    """Yield (url, lastmod) pairs, recursing into  files."""
    seen = seen if seen is not None else set()
    if sitemap_url in seen or len(seen) >= max_sitemaps:
        return
    seen.add(sitemap_url)
    root = ET.fromstring(fetch(sitemap_url))
    if root.tag == f"{NS}sitemapindex":
        for loc in root.iter(f"{NS}loc"):
            yield from walk(loc.text.strip(), seen, max_sitemaps)
    else:
        for u in root.iter(f"{NS}url"):
            lastmod = u.findtext(f"{NS}lastmod")
            yield u.findtext(f"{NS}loc").strip(), lastmod

def status(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA, method="HEAD")
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
            return url, r.status
    except HTTPError as e:
        return url, e.code
    except URLError as e:
        return url, f"error: {e.reason}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    site = "https://crawlee.dev"
    urls = []
    for sm in find_sitemaps(site):
        urls.extend(walk(sm))
    print(f"{len(urls)} URLs found")
    sample = [u for u, _ in urls[:50]]
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
        for url, code in pool.map(status, sample):
            if code != 200:
                print(code, url)
    print("checked", len(sample))

What it does:

  • Discovery: reads the Sitemap: lines from robots.txt and falls back to /sitemap.xml.
  • Gzip: checks the first two bytes (1f 8b) instead of trusting headers or file extensions. Some servers send .xml.gz files as application/octet-stream, and others gzip a file called .xml.
  • Sitemap indexes: if the root tag is , it recurses into every , with a seen set and a limit so a misconfigured index can't loop forever.
  • Status codes: sends parallel HEAD requests. Redirects are followed, so a 200 here means "200 after redirects".

Running it against https://crawlee.dev found 4,861 URLs in about a second. To be sure the index and gzip paths work, I also tested it against a local sitemap index pointing to one .xml.gz and one plain .xml child:

[('http://127.0.0.1:8777/sitemap.xml', '2026-11-01'), ('http://127.0.0.1:8777/missing', None)]
[('http://127.0.0.1:8777/sitemap.xml', 200), ('http://127.0.0.1:8777/missing', 404)]

Where the DIY version falls short

  • HEAD is sometimes rejected (405) or treated differently from GET. A robust checker falls back to GET.
  • 200 after redirects hides the fact that the sitemap lists URLs that redirect, which is an SEO issue in itself. Record the final URL and a "redirected" flag.
  • Sites without robots.txt entries often use /sitemap_index.xml or /wp-sitemap.xml (WordPress), not just /sitemap.xml.
  • Large sites have millions of URLs, so you want filters (/blog/ only, lastmod in the last 30 days) before checking status codes.
  • comes in several formats (2026-11-01, 2026-11-01T10:00:00+01:00, …), so normalise it before filtering.

All of these are fixable. That list is exactly what I ended up building into the Actor below.

2. Hosted option: Sitemap URL Extractor on Apify

The Sitemap URL Extractor takes homepages or sitemap URLs. It:

  • discovers sitemaps via robots.txt and common paths,
  • handles indexes and gzip,
  • filters by include/exclude patterns and lastmod, and
  • can check every URL's status with HEAD, falling back to GET.

The output is a dataset you can download as CSV, JSON or Excel, or read from code.

Each row looks like this (a real row from the run above, shortened):

There are also image and video counts, hreflang alternates and news titles when the sitemap has them.

title: How to fetch German job listings from the Bundesagentur für Arbeit API with Python and Node.js (no scraping)
summary:
Germany's federal employment agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) runs the country's biggest job board, with hundreds of thousands of open positions. If you're building a job alert, a salary analysis or a dashboard of who's hiring in your city, you don't need to scrape HTML. The website runs on a JSON API you can call yourself.

This post covers:

  1. Calling the API directly with Python (requests) and Node.js (fetch).
  2. The pitfalls you'll hit once you go past a quick demo.
  3. A ready-made Apify Actor that handles them, if you'd rather not maintain that part yourself.

Disclosure: I built the Actor in part 3 (Arbeitsagentur Jobs API on Apify). Parts 1 and 2 work without it.

1. The raw API

The job search at arbeitsagentur.de/jobsuche calls this endpoint:

GET https://rest.arbeitsagentur.de/jobboerse/jobsuche-service/pc/v6/jobs
Header: X-API-Key: jobboerse-jobsuche

The X-API-Key isn't a personal secret. It's the public client ID the agency's own web app sends, and the community-maintained bundesAPI/jobsuche-api project documents it too. You don't need to sign up for anything.

Useful query parameters:

Parameter Meaning
was What: keywords or a job title (Python, Pflegefachkraft, …)
wo Where: a city or postcode
umkreis Radius in km around wo
veroeffentlichtseit Only postings from the last n days (0–100)
size, page Paging (page starts at 1)

Python 

import base64
import requests

BASE = "https://rest.arbeitsagentur.de/jobboerse/jobsuche-service"
HEADERS = {"X-API-Key": "jobboerse-jobsuche"}  # public client id used by the official web app

def search(was, wo, umkreis=25, veroeffentlichtseit=7, size=50, max_pages=3):
    for page in range(1, max_pages + 1):
        r = requests.get(f"{BASE}/pc/v6/jobs", headers=HEADERS, timeout=30, params={
            "was": was, "wo": wo, "umkreis": umkreis,
            "veroeffentlichtseit": veroeffentlichtseit, "size": size, "page": page,
        })
        r.raise_for_status()
        data = r.json()
        jobs = data.get("ergebnisliste", [])
        yield from jobs
        if page * size >= int(data.get("maxErgebnisse", 0)) or not jobs:
            break

for job in search("Python", "Berlin", max_pages=1, size=5):
    loc = job.get("stellenlokationen", [{}])[0].get("adresse", {})
    ref = job["referenznummer"]
    print(job["stellenangebotsTitel"], "|", job.get("firma"), "|", loc.get("ort"),
          "|", f"https://www.arbeitsagentur.de/jobsuche/jobdetail/{ref}")

# Details for a single posting: the reference number goes base64-encoded into the path
detail_id = base64.b64encode(ref.encode()).decode()
d = requests.get(f"{BASE}/pc/v4/jobdetails/{detail_id}", headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
print("detail status:", d.status_code, "| keys:", sorted(d.json())[:8] if d.ok else d.text[:100])

Output (03.11.2026, shortened):

Senior Python Developer – Microservices & Data Pipelines (m/w/d) | BWI GmbH | Berlin | https://www.arbeitsagentur.de/jobsuche/jobdetail/12336-a26f539j0456738-S
Versuchsingenieur (m/w/d) | FERCHAU GmbH Niederlassung Berlin | Berlin | https://www.arbeitsagentur.de/jobsuche/jobdetail/12265-485458_JB5289084-S
...
detail status: 200 | keys: ['aenderungsdatum', 'allianzpartnerName', 'allianzpartnerUrl', ...]

Node.js (18+, no dependencies) 

const BASE = 'https://rest.arbeitsagentur.de/jobboerse/jobsuche-service';
const headers = { 'X-API-Key': 'jobboerse-jobsuche' };

const params = new URLSearchParams({
    was: 'Python', wo: 'Berlin', umkreis: '25', veroeffentlichtseit: '7', size: '5', page: '1',

A one-off query is easy. A pipeline that runs every day for months hits these:

  • Contact data is personal data. Descriptions often contain recruiters' e-mail addresses and phone numbers. If you don't need them, don't store them (GDPR).

I needed this pipeline myself, so I packaged it as an Apify Actor. It:

  • automatically splits nationwide searches over 10,000 results by federal state,
  • maps the output to flat, English field names, with salary as {type, period, min, max},
  • fetches details concurrently (optional, includeDetails),
  • remembers postings it has already seen (onlyNew), and

export APIFY_TOKEN=your_token_here

Usage: APIFY_TOKEN=... python jobs_to_csv.py
"""

import os

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("paperlinenstudio/arbeitsagentur-jobs-api").call(
    run_input={
        "keywords": ["Python Entwickler"],
        "locations": ["Berlin"],
        "radiusKm": 25,
        "publishedWithinDays": 7,  # only jobs from the last week
        "maxItems": 20,
    }
)
jobs = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())

with open("jobs.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["title", "employer", "city", "salary_min", "salary_max", "published", "url"])

            job["employer"],

title: Can You Get a Bama Bound AI Video in 1080p? What Upscaling a 480p or 720p Clip Actually Does, Measured With ffmpeg SSIM and PSNR
summary:
November 3, 2026. I build bamabound.app, a small studio that turns one photo into the eight-second "I'M BAMA BOUND" field-banner clip at 480p or 720p. People keep asking whether they can get it in 1080p. This post is my honest answer, with a test you can rerun.

Short answer: not from my studio. The FAQ says it plainly: "There is no prompt, no duration control and no 1080p option" (FAQ). You can upscale the file to 1080x1920 with one ffmpeg command, and some editing apps will do it anyway. But upscaling makes the frame bigger. It doesn't add detail. In my test, going from 480p to 720p at generation time did more for the banner letters than any upscaler did afterwards. If the letters matter to you, pick 720p ($9.99 instead of $7.99, pricing). Don't count on 1080p rescuing a 480p file.

Why the resolution is decided at generation time

An image-to-video model renders the clip at a fixed pixel grid. For this meme the hard part of that grid is the banner: three words in white on red, on fabric that moves while the person jumps. Each letter gets some number of pixels at render time, and that's all the detail it will ever have. A later scaler can only interpolate between those pixels. It can't learn what the letter edge "should" have been.

So the 480p/720p choice really asks how many pixels the model gets to draw the person and the banner. That's also why the 480p vs 720p guide suggests 720p "if you expect to crop it later". A crop throws pixels away, and you can't get them back.

I wanted numbers rather than adjectives, so I measured it.

The test

You can't measure an upscale against a real 1080p "truth" you don't have. So I made one:

  1. A synthetic 1080x1920, 8-second, 30 fps clip. It has a green field with per-frame noise for texture, a red strip, and white I'M BAMA BOUND letters that bob 40 px up and down inside it. No person, and no generator output.
